content: Health workers and healthcare facilities must ensure that the diagnostic kits they use are of high quality and have undergone proper quality assurance processes. They should also implement robust quality management systems and post-market surveillance mechanisms to identify and report any quality issues that may arise. The needs of the population being served should be carefully considered. While many individuals can perform self-testing with minimal or no assistance, some users may require additional support. Programs should develop concise on-site demonstrations and create support resources that can be shared with self-testers in person, as well as through videos or messaging platforms. In resource-limited settings, instructional videos and virtual interventions may be prioritized, or group demonstrations may be organized to efficiently cater to larger populations with minimal supervision and time investment. Syphilis self-testing should be made accessible to sexually active adolescents. To facilitate this, countries need to review and revise their national age-of-consent policies. This effort can be coordinated across related health areas, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), HIV, and broader sexual and reproductive health services. Prevention and treatment services should be tailored to meet the needs of different age groups. Health workers should deliver messages about syphilis self-testing that are specifically adapted for adolescents, emphasizing autonomy and self-care. Integration opportunities should be explored. Individuals who may benefit from syphilis self-testing often face ongoing risks related to other STIs, including HIV and viral hepatitis. Programs should consider integrating services based on the epidemiological context and available resources. For instance, dual HIV/syphilis self-testing could be leveraged, along with fully integrated messaging, demand generation, service delivery, and referral pathways to treatment and care. Ongoing monitoring and evaluation are critical. The implementation of syphilis self-testing should be routinely monitored and reported as part of the national health response. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises countries to adopt pragmatic approaches, such as triangulating data from standard HIV testing and treatment records with HIV self-test distribution data. Monitoring and evaluation strategies for syphilis self-testing can be adapted from existing self-care and self-testing measurement tools. Programs should regularly review these data and apply lessons learned to optimize their strategies. Collaboration with a range of stakeholders, including communities and networks of key populations disproportionately affected by syphilis and other STIs, is essential to identify priorities and inform the design, implementation, and monitoring of research efforts and outcomes. Research priorities for syphilis testing include conducting geographically representative studies across diverse populations, particularly in high-prevalence groups. Different testing algorithms and strategies should be assessed, along with pathways for treatment and care following diagnosis. Implementation research in resource-limited settings, involving community-based delivery by lay providers, is also needed. The use of dual treponemal/non-treponemal rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for self-testing should be adapted and trialed. Budget impact analyses should be conducted to evaluate the affordability of dual RDTs in various populations and settings, considering program budgets. Barriers and facilitators on both the provider and user sides should be better understood to design optimal services. Social harms associated with self-testing should be monitored using existing systems in real-world settings. Syphilis self-testing should be evaluated for its performance at different stages of infection and in various clinical and treatment histories. The best algorithms and testing strategies for dual RDTs should be identified, and their adaptation for self-testing should be explored. The affordability, cost-effectiveness, and cost-saving potential of dual RDTs in different contexts and populations should be assessed. The impact of dual RDTs on time to treatment initiation and loss to follow-up should be studied. Barriers and facilitators for adoption and scale-up should be identified, and the potential for social harms in different populations and contexts should be evaluated. Partner services for STIs are a critical component of quality case management. Many STIs, such as gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis, can be asymptomatic, making partner services an effective way to detect and treat undiagnosed infections. WHO recommends offering a range of voluntary partner service options tailored to individual needs and preferences as part of a comprehensive STI testing, care, and prevention package. These services must always be voluntary, with strict protection of patient privacy and confidentiality. Enhanced patient referral, delayed provider referral, and provider-assisted referral are among the approaches that have shown the greatest impact and should be prioritized where feasible and acceptable. Expedited partner therapy (EPT) may also be considered for curable STIs like chlamydia and gonorrhea. Linkage to STI management services for sexual partners is essential to ensure appropriate care and prevention. The WHO emphasizes the importance of offering a variety of partner service options to address the global burden of STIs, with millions of new cases reported daily. Approaches with provider support are particularly effective and should be encouraged where resources allow.
